execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: true editor: visual --- # Caveat emptor ## Caveats I will be showing you what you can do, not what you should do
. . . Creating LLM tools for phenotyping is relatively easy. Creating tools that improves the quality of research and provides a good user experience is hard
. . . Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, for which task.
. . . System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.
. . . Closed-weight models often show performance drift, making validation even harder. ## More caveats Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Antrhropic, etc)
. . . And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources)
. . . ## Even more caveats Low quality health research is prevalent
. . . Reproducibility crisis in health research
. . . LLM integration can go both ways. Increasing risk of OMOP-slop vs additional context and double-checking. # Working with LLMs from R ## ellmer We'll be using the ellmer R package for interacting with LLMs.
. . . Provides a simple interface for working with LLMs in a consistent manner.
. . . Relying on ellmer, we can build generic LLM support with users choosing the model to use. ## Unstructured chat ellmer supports various popular providers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- chat_anthropic() chat <- chat_deepseek() chat <- chat_google_gemini() chat <- chat_mistral() chat <- chat_openai() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_google_gemini() |> dplyr::pull("id") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "antigravity-preview-05-2026" [2] "antigravity-preview-09-2026" [3] "antigravity-preview-latest" [4] "deep-research-max-preview-04-2026" [5] "deep-research-preview-04-2026" [6] "deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025" [7] "gemini-2.5-computer-use-preview-10-2025" [8] "gemini-2.5-flash" [9] "gemini-2.5-flash-image" [10] "gemini-2.5-flash-lite" [11] "gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts" [12] "gemini-2.5-pro" [13] "gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts" [14] "gemini-3-flash-preview" [15] "gemini-3-pro-image" [16] "gemini-3-pro-image-preview" [17] "gemini-3.1-flash-image" [18] "gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview" [19] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite" [20] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image" [21] "gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview" [22] "gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview" [23] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview" [24] "gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools" [25] "gemini-3.5-flash" [26] "gemini-3.5-flash-lite" [27] "gemini-3.5-transcribe" [28] "gemini-3.6-flash" [29] "gemini-3.7-flash" [30] "gemini-3.8-flash" [31] "gemini-3.8-flash-lite-tts" [32] "gemini-3.8-flash-tts" [33] "gemini-4-argon" [34] "gemini-flash-latest" [35] "gemini-flash-lite-latest" [36] "gemini-nano-banana-2.1" [37] "gemini-omni-1.1-flash" [38] "gemini-omni-flash-preview" [39] "gemini-pro-latest" [40] "gemini-robotics-er-2-preview" [41] "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it" [42] "gemma-4-31b-it" [43] "lyria-3-clip-preview" [44] "lyria-3-pro-preview" [45] "lyria-3.5" [46] "nano-banana-pro-preview" ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Similarly we can work with local models ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat <- chat_ollama() ``` :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ellmer::models_ollama() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` id created_at size capabilities 1 MedGemma:4b 2026-10-14 3338942556 completion,vision 2 gemma3:4b 2026-10-14 3350272403 completion,vision 3 qwen2.5:0.5b 2026-10-14 397821319 completion,tools 4 gemma3:1b 2026-10-14 806067407 completion ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat I'm going to be using local MedGemma 4B today. You can choose a model you have access to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(dplyr) library(PhenotypeR) sytem_prompt <- "You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based." chat_medgemma <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = sytem_prompt ) chat_medgemma ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ── system ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── You are an expert clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat We can work with have a simple, unstructured, chat. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension's clinical presentation is diverse, ranging from asymptomatic to severe end-organ damage. Key features include: * **Elevated blood pressure readings:** Defined by consistent elevated measurements (e.g., systolic ≥140 mmHg, diastolic ≥90 mmHg according to current guidelines). * **Symptoms:** Can be absent (asymptomatic) or associated with headaches, dizziness, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, chest pain, or visual disturbances. * **Risk factors:** Including age, family history, race, obesity, lack of physical activity, diet high in sodium/low in potassium, excessive alcohol consumption, tobacco use, chronic kidney disease, and sleep apnea. * **End-organ damage (target organ damage - TOD):** Evidence of damage to the heart, brain, kidneys, or eyes leading to specific clinical manifestations. * **Diagnosis confirmation:** Diagnosed using multiple blood pressure measurements over time, ideally from ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). **Important Considerations:** * **Pre-hypertension:** Defined as a systolic blood pressure between 120 to 139 mmHg and a diastolic blood pressure between 80 to 89 mmHg. This population requires monitoring. * **White coat hypertension:** Elevated blood pressure in a clinical setting, but normal readings at home. * **Masked hypertension:** Normal blood pressure in a clinical setting, but elevated blood pressure at home. * **Clinical decision points**: The severity of hypertension is determined by the presence of target organ damage. I am an AI and cannot provide medical advice. Consult with qualified healthcare professionals for diagnosis and treatment of hypertension. ``` ::: :::
. . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What are the demographics of people presenting with of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension demographics vary across populations and are influenced by socioeconomic factors, lifestyle, and access to care. Here's a general overview: * **Age:** Hypertension risk increases with age, with higher prevalence in older adults. * **Sex/Gender:** Hypertension is more common in men than women, but the gap narrows with age. * **Race/Ethnicity:** Hypertension prevalence varies considerably across racial and ethnic groups, with higher rates observed in African Americans, Hispanic/Latinx populations, and some Asian populations. * **Socioeconomic Status:** Lower socioeconomic status is associated with higher hypertension prevalence, potentially due to factors like limited access to healthy food, safe environments for physical activity, and healthcare. * **Geographic Location:** Hypertension prevalence differs globally, influenced by lifestyle habits, dietary patterns, and socioeconomic conditions specific to regions. It is essential to acknowledge these demographic disparities and address them through targeted interventions and health promotion programs. ``` ::: ::: ## Unstructured chat Bad idea: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("What clinical codes should I use to identify hypertension in my OMOP CDM?") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` In the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM), hypertension is typically identified using a combination of diagnosis and procedure codes. Here are the primary codes used: * **ICD-10:** * **I10** - Essential (primary) hypertension * **I15** - Secondary hypertension due to kidney disease * **I16** - Essential (primary) hypertension due to kidney disease * **I17** - Essential (primary) hypertension due to renal artery stenosis * **I18** - Essential (primary) hypertension due to drug or endocrine use * **I19** - Other specified hypertension * **I25** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy * **I25.0** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy * **I25.1** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure * **I25.2** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and impaired left ventricular systolic function * **I25.3** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and other heart diseases * **I25.4** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction * **I25.5** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and other heart diseases * **I25.6** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and unspecified heart disease * **I25.7** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and other heart diseases * **I25.8** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and other heart diseases * **I25.9** - Hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy and unspecified heart disease * **I26** - Hypertension with heart failure * **CPT (Procedure Codes):** *While not directly diagnostic,* hypertension is often identified from procedures related to blood pressure monitoring, such as: * **99213:** Home blood pressure monitoring * **99214:** Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring **Key Considerations for OMOP CDM:** * **Multiple Codes:** You will likely use *multiple* codes to represent the diagnosis of hypertension, particularly for secondary forms. * **Hierarchy:** In the OMOP CDM, you'll need to consider the hierarchy of codes. For example, I10 is the primary code for essential hypertension, while I15 is a secondary code for hypertension due to kidney disease. * **Missing Values:** Be prepared to handle missing values for these codes. Consider the implications of these missing values for your downstream analyses. * **Context is Key:** Always interpret codes within the clinical context of the patient's record. Therefore, you would select the relevant ICD-10 diagnostic codes (e.g., I10, I15) and potentially associated CPT codes based on the information available in the patient's record. The choice of codes will depend on the specific data available and the research question being addressed. ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Instead of allowing freedom in output, we can instead force results to be returned in a specific structured format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", type = type_object( typical_symptoms = type_string("summarise typical symptoms"), confirmatory_test = type_string("summarise what test result would confirm diagnosis"), disqualifying_diagnoses = type_string("summarise what alternative diagnoses need to be ruled out") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $typical_symptoms [1] "Symptoms of hypertension can be absent (asymptomatic) or associated with headaches, dizziness, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, chest pain, or visual disturbances." $confirmatory_test [1] "Diagnosed using multiple blood pressure measurements over time, ideally from ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM)." $disqualifying_diagnoses [1] "Symptoms would be less likely if the patient with hypertension also has other, more obvious conditions causing the listed symptoms." ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Instead of allowing freedom in output, we can instead force results to be returned in a specific structured format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "What are the demographics of people presenting with of hypertension", type = type_object( average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("What is the average age at diagnosis?"), proportion_male = type_number("What proportion (between 0 and 1) of patients diagnosed with hypertension are male?") ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $average_age_at_diagnosis [1] 60 $proportion_male [1] 0.55 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat Remember, even with the same model you can get different results! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = sytem_prompt ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 35 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 50 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 ``` ::: ::: ## Structured chat We can set temperature to zero and add a seed to get closer to reproducibility. (This generally works better for local models than when working with cloud models.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = sytem_prompt, params = params(temperature = 0, seed = 42) ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 ``` ::: ::: # Integrating LLMs with PheontypeR ## Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models - Available to all of the OHDSI community
. . . - Smoother package development (easy to implement, cheaper, and straightforward to test)
. . . - Easy to switch to using frontier models (and see if they are worth the extra cost).
. . . - But 6+ months behind "state-of-the-art". (Although allows us to learn from experience of others) ## Human-in-the-loop - Designed to support the human phenotyper.
. . . - Able to review and edit LLM output
. . . - Main use of LLM is too provide additional context making it easier to double-check results ## Phenotyping tasks > "A problem well stated is a problem half solved." > > Charles F. Kettering (1876 – 1958)
. . . Nowadays, a problem well stated is a problem 95% solved. ## Phenotyping tasks Started with lower-stakes, human-in-the-loop, phenotyping tasks: - Drafting clinical descriptions . . . - Reviewing codes included that led to cohort inclusion . . . - Contextualising PhenotypeR results . . . Higher-risk tasks currently out-of-scope: - Searching for codes. . . . - Creating cohort logic. . . . - End-to-end phenotyping # Clinical descriptions ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clinicalDescriptionSpecification() |> listviewer::jsonedit() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyClinicalDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, "hypertension", tempdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//RtmpyTpH8E/hypertension.json ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $hypertension $hypertension$introduction_synonyms [1] "Hypertension is a medical condition characterized by elevated blood pressure, typically defined as a systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or higher or a diastolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or higher. Other synonyms include high blood pressure and arterial hypertension. These terms are frequently used interchangeably in medical and public health contexts." $hypertension$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms [1] "Hypertension is often asymptomatic, with many individuals unaware they have the condition until it is detected during a routine medical examination. When symptoms do occur, they may include severe headache, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, and dizziness. In some cases, hypertension can lead to complications affecting the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. These complications can manifest as chest pain, palpitations, irregular heartbeat, stroke, kidney failure, vision problems or blindness." $hypertension$epidemiology [1] "The prevalence of hypertension increases with age, with the highest rates observed in older adults. It is more common in men than women, particularly before menopause, but the prevalence is similar between the sexes after menopause. Hypertension is also more common in people of African descent than in people of European descent. Some modifiable risk factors include high sodium intake, obesity, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol consumption. Non-modifiable risk factors include age, sex, and genetics. Common comorbidities that may precede or follow a diagnosis of hypertension include cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and peripheral artery disease. These conditions can either be a cause or consequence of the elevated blood pressure." $hypertension$assessment_diagnosis [1] "Individuals suspected of having hypertension may undergo a medical examination to assess their blood pressure. Blood pressure is typically measured using a sphygmomanometer, with readings recorded as systolic pressure (the pressure when the heart beats) and diastolic pressure (the pressure when the heart rests between beats). A diagnosis of hypertension is usually made when blood pressure readings are consistently elevated on multiple occasions. Additional tests may be performed to rule out other conditions that can cause hypertension or to evaluate its effects on the body. These tests may include urine tests, blood tests, electrocardiogram (ECG), and echocardiogram." $hypertension$therapeutic_plan_treatment [1] "The initial treatment for hypertension typically involves lifestyle modifications, such as reducing sodium intake, increasing physical activity, losing weight, and limiting alcohol consumption. Medications may be prescribed if lifestyle changes are not sufficient to control blood pressure. Common medications used to treat hypertension include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers. The choice of medication depends on individual patient characteristics, such as age, other medical conditions, and potential side effects. If blood pressure is uncontrolled with a single medication, a combination of drugs may be used. Further medications may be prescribed if initial treatment is not successful or if other medical conditions require treatment." $hypertension$complications_prognosis [1] "Hypertension can lead to a number of serious complications, including heart attack, stroke, kidney failure, heart failure, vision loss, and peripheral artery disease. The risk of these complications increases with the severity and duration of hypertension. The prognosis for people with hypertension depends on the presence and severity of complications, as well as adherence to treatment. Effective management of hypertension can significantly reduce the risk of developing complications and improve long-term outcomes. The prognosis for people with hypertension is generally better with earlier diagnosis and treatment." $hypertension$disqualifiers [1] "Other conditions that can cause elevated blood pressure include renal artery stenosis, pheochromocytoma, and hyperaldosteronism. It is important to rule out these conditions when evaluating individuals with hypertension, particularly those with atypical or resistant hypertension. These conditions can also be considered in cases where the patient presents with specific symptoms that are more suggestive of a secondary cause of hypertension, such as headache, flushing, or sweating. The temporality of these findings is typically assessed, and if the symptoms are present at the same time as elevated blood pressure, it is more likely that the elevated blood pressure is a primary problem." ``` ::: ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, c("Primary hypertension", "Secondary hypertension", "Resistant hypertension"), tempdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for Primary hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'Primary hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//RtmpyTpH8E/Primary hypertension.json Getting clinical description for Secondary hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'Secondary hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//RtmpyTpH8E/Secondary hypertension.json Getting clinical description for Resistant hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'Resistant hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//RtmpyTpH8E/Resistant hypertension.json ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd$`Primary hypertension`$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Primary hypertension is characterized by chronically elevated blood pressure, with no identifiable secondary cause. Other synonyms include Essential hypertension, malignant hypertension, and white coat hypertension." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd$`Secondary hypertension`$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Secondary hypertension is defined as hypertension that results from a known underlying cause. It is also referred to as secondary blood pressure, essential hypertension, and hypertensive disorder of pregnancy." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd$`Resistant hypertension`$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure that remains above target levels despite the use of three antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic, at optimal doses." ``` ::: ::: ## Extra context: data source descriptions Data partner descriptions can be used to provide extra context ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyDataSourceDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: # Reviewing codes ## Reviewing codes To do # Contextualising PhenotypeR results ## Contextualising PhenotypeR results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_exp <- getCohortExpectations(chat_medgemma, "hypertension", tempdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting expectations for hypertension Exporting CSV with expectations for hypertension ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//RtmpyTpH8E/expectations.csv ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_exp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 5 cohort_name estimate value diagnostics source 1 hypertension Clinical description Hypertensi… cohort_cou… MedGe… 2 hypertension Frequency Hypertensi… cohort_cou… MedGe… 3 hypertension Median age of incident cases 50 to 60 (… cohort_cha… MedGe… 4 hypertension Percentage male 50% to 60%… cohort_cha… MedGe… 5 hypertension Survival at five years 70% to 80%… cohort_sur… MedGe… 6 hypertension Frequently seen comorbidities Coronary a… large_scal… MedGe… 7 hypertension Frequently seen signs and symptoms Elevated s… large_scal… MedGe… 8 hypertension Frequently seen medications Antihypert… large_scal… MedGe… ``` ::: ::: ## <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
